papers.title: DeepEdu-v1: Efficient and Scalable Agentic LLMs for Vietnamese Education
papers.authors: Quang Nguyen, Hieu Nguyen, Hien Hoang, Toan Pham, Cong Tran, Nam Vu
papers.abstract: AI tutoring could markedly improve learning outcomes for students in developing regions such as Vietnam, yet the two obvious paths both fall short. Cloud assistants such as ChatGPT route sensitive student data to foreign servers---violating data-sovereignty laws such as Vietnam's Decree 53---and, pre-trained on Western-centric corpora, are not organized around the national textbook curriculum, so their knowledge of local content is unsystematic and frequently hallucinated. Self-hosting an open model keeps data on-premise but hits a two-fold wall: post-training quantization (AWQ, GPTQ) tames the static weight footprint, yet the dynamic KV cache and prefill latency of long tutoring contexts still cause out-of-memory failures and slow responses on consumer GPUs, while the model keeps hallucinating on region-specific material. We present DeepEdu-v1, an AI-tutoring system for Vietnamese education built on SCALE (Self-improving Context-Aware Learning Engine), a framework with two innovations. First, a long-context inference engine amortizes token selection from per-sub-chunk to per-cluster granularity; on long-context retrieval it issues x7.7 fewer retrieval calls than a state-of-the-art selective-attention baseline, cutting prefill latency (TTFT) by roughly 35% while matching or improving task accuracy. Second, a self-improving agentic layer continuously curates a verified playbook from past interactions instead of fine-tuning, a design intended to progressively reduce reliance on dominant-language priors as trustworthy local knowledge accumulates. In its deployed configuration, DeepEdu achieves a nearly x2 TTFT speedup over standard vLLM serving and lifts agentic accuracy from 70.0% to 79.5% on complex tasks, with the strongest per-track gains across financial-reasoning and interactive-agent benchmarks.
takeaways: DeepEdu-v1 is an AI tutoring system for Vietnamese education built on SCALE, combining a long-context inference engine with a self-improving agentic layer to better handle local curriculum content and reduce hallucinations.

On long-context retrieval, the system uses per-cluster token selection to make x7.7 fewer retrieval calls than a selective-attention baseline, cutting TTFT by about 35% while matching or improving task accuracy.

The deployed system nearly doubles TTFT speed over standard vLLM serving and raises agentic accuracy from 70.0% to 79.5%, suggesting more practical on-premise tutoring for consumer GPUs under data-sovereignty constraints.
actionItems: Review the SCALE long-context inference design and the self-improving playbook mechanism to verify how they address Vietnamese curriculum grounding and data-sovereignty constraints.
Evaluate DeepEdu-v1 against a standard vLLM baseline on long-context tutoring tasks, measuring TTFT, retrieval-call count, and agentic accuracy on complex education examples.
Assess whether the system’s verified playbook can remain reliable and curricularly aligned over time without fine-tuning, especially for region-specific content and consumer-GPU deployment.

papers.title: Muslim: A Deployed Arabic Voice AI Platform for Grounded Islamic Knowledge
papers.abstract: We present Muslim, a production Arabic voice AI platform serving grounded, sourced Islamic knowledge to real users. Beyond a real-time voice pipeline (NeMo Arabic ASR, an OpenAI-compatible LLM endpoint, self-hosted TTS) and a deterministic multi-source retrieval layer routed across six Model Context Protocol servers, we report three things a research prototype typically lacks. First, a released family of fine-tuned Arabic Islamic model artifacts: an efficient tool-routing LLM (Muslim-6B-PRO, 5.94B parameters) and a Modern Standard Arabic TTS model (Fasih-TTS-V1) that ranks 5th of 17 overall and 2nd of 11 open-weight systems on the community-voted Arabic TTS Arena for MSA. Second, an account and metering layer - a free per-account turn allowance, capacity-aware refusal, and email verification deferred to the point it actually matters - that turns an open demo into an operable, abuse-resistant product. Third, a three-layer observability stack (liveness, error reporting, product analytics) built specifically around the system's characteristic failure mode: a GPU-bound agent host going silent while the web tier keeps serving normally. We report real, measured latency and accuracy figures (98.4% recitation-validation accuracy on 124 cases; end-to-end voice latency of 0.9-1.7s) and discuss the concrete engineering trade-offs and limitations of running an Islamic-knowledge voice product in production.
takeaways: Deployed Arabic voice AI platform, Muslim, delivering grounded, sourced Islamic knowledge through a real-time voice system and production product stack.

Method/evidence: combines NeMo Arabic ASR, an OpenAI-compatible LLM endpoint, self-hosted TTS, and deterministic multi-source retrieval across six MCP servers; reports 98.4% recitation-validation accuracy on 124 cases and 0.9–1.7s end-to-end latency.

Practical implication: releases fine-tuned Arabic artifacts (Muslim-6B-PRO and Fasih-TTS-V1) plus abuse-resistant account/metering and observability layers for operating an open, production Islamic-knowledge voice service.
actionItems: Review the grounding and retrieval design across the six MCP servers to verify that sourced Islamic answers are consistently tied to the retrieved references in the deployed voice flow.

Evaluate the released Arabic artifacts and system pipeline by reproducing the reported 98.4% recitation-validation accuracy on 124 cases and the 0.9–1.7s end-to-end latency under production-like load.

Assess whether the account/metering, capacity-aware refusal, and deferred email verification are sufficient to prevent abuse without blocking legitimate users of the open Islamic-knowledge voice service.

papers.title: Highlight-Then-Summarize: Learning to Compress Evidence for Long-Context Understanding
papers.authors: Zhaoyuan Xia, Qinghongbing Xie, Yung Xiang Hue, Jianguang Jiang, Gaofeng Lu, Zhenyu Jiao, Xing Yuan, Dai Dai, Tong Mo, Long Zeng
papers.abstract: Long-context understanding requires large language models (LLMs) to reason over lengthy documents, conversations, and code, yet task-relevant evidence is often sparse and scattered amid substantial irrelevant and redundant content. We propose Highlight-Then-Summarize (H2S), a compress-then-reason paradigm that first identifies source-grounded, question-relevant evidence and then integrates it into a compact, question-conditioned summary before producing the final answer. To train this behavior, we construct H2S-Dataset, comprising 6,647 examples from 11 benchmark families with an average context length of 43.9K tokens, and introduce H2S-RL, which provides process-level rewards for evidence selection and summary construction in addition to final-answer correctness. We evaluate on H2S-Bench, a seven-task long-context suite. Under a shared 128K input and 4K output budget, H2S-14B achieves an average score of 32.60, outperforming Qwen3.8-27B by 10.17 points and obtaining the strongest overall result among the evaluated open-source models. H2S-14B also achieves the highest Evidence-Summary Quality score and retains 97.1% of its 16K-budget performance with only a 4K output budget. These results show that explicitly selecting and integrating evidence improves long-context reasoning while enabling more compact generation.
takeaways: Introduces Highlight-Then-Summarize (H2S), a compress-then-reason method that first selects source-grounded, question-relevant evidence and then builds a compact, question-conditioned summary before answering.

Trains on H2S-Dataset with 6,647 examples across 11 benchmark families and uses H2S-RL with process-level rewards for evidence selection, summary construction, and final-answer correctness; evaluates on H2S-Bench.

Under a 128K input and 4K output budget, H2S-14B tops evaluated open-source models, improving average score and evidence-summary quality while retaining 97.1% of its 16K-budget performance, implying better long-context reasoning with shorter outputs.
actionItems: Review the H2S training setup and H2S-Bench evaluation protocol, with attention to how source-grounded evidence selection and summary construction are defined and rewarded.

Run an ablation or comparative evaluation against a strong long-context baseline under the same 128K input and 4K output budget to test whether process-level rewards improve final-answer accuracy and evidence-summary quality.

Assess whether the compress-then-reason approach depends on reliable evidence highlighting and whether it can be adopted without introducing missing-evidence or over-compression risks in long-context tasks.

papers.title: Can You Check That? The Checkability Boundary for Local LLM Network Automation
papers.abstract: Sending every network-automation input to a third-party frontier LLM exports sensitive artifacts such as production configurations, topologies, and logs. Querying small language models (SLMs) locally avoids this egress, but SLM outputs can be error-prone for direct use. This work introduces checkability as a criterion for determining which tasks are suitable for local inference. A task is checkable when it exposes a cheap, deterministic test - an intrinsic check - that rejects outputs violating a necessary correctness condition. We instantiate this idea in Touchstone, a local-first pipeline that uses seven off-the-shelf SLMs (1-8B parameters) to generate candidates, uses task-specific intrinsic checks to reject responses, and escalates unresolved inputs to a frontier LLM. On conflict detection and intent translation tasks, Touchstone reaches 98.6% and 93.8% end-to-end accuracy while escalating only 16% and 17% of inputs, respectively. On TeleQnA, a knowledge-only control that has no task-specific intrinsic checks, Touchstone is unable to match the accuracy of the frontier baseline. Our results support a simple deployment rule: keep inference local when task semantics support precise, low-cost checks; escalate the rest.
takeaways: Introduces "checkability" as a criterion for deciding when network-automation tasks can be handled locally: a task is checkable if it has a cheap, deterministic intrinsic test that can reject outputs violating a necessary correctness condition.

Implements Touchstone, a local-first pipeline that uses seven off-the-shelf 1–8B SLMs to generate candidates, applies task-specific intrinsic checks to filter them, and escalates unresolved inputs to a frontier LLM; reports 98.6% end-to-end accuracy on conflict detection and 93.8% on intent translation while escalating 16% and 17% of inputs.

Practical takeaway: keep inference local when task semantics support precise, low-cost checks, and escalate tasks without such checks; the TeleQnA control without task-specific intrinsic checks did not match the frontier baseline.
actionItems: Review the checkability criterion and the Touchstone pipeline for your network-automation workflows to identify tasks with cheap, deterministic intrinsic checks versus tasks that should be escalated.

Run a local-first benchmark using off-the-shelf 1–8B SLMs with task-specific intrinsic checks on conflict detection and intent translation, and compare end-to-end accuracy and escalation rates against a frontier LLM baseline.
Assess whether each target task has a precise low-cost intrinsic check; if not, question whether local inference is appropriate or whether routing sensitive inputs to a frontier model is necessary.

papers.title: Prompt Minimization: Reducing Input Redundancy Without Sacrificing Output Fidelity
papers.authors: Marius F. R. Juston, Kevin A. Karim, Jonathan Gao, Kevin C. Li, Rudhi Bashambu
papers.abstract: Despite the growing capabilities of large language models (LLMs), prompt design remains largely heuristic and ad hoc. This project will explore $\textit{prompt minimization}$, the process of reducing prompts to their smallest, most information-dense form while preserving output fidelity. Practically, shorter prompts reduce computational overhead and inference latency, especially when large contexts, such as entire documents or codebases, are included unnecessarily. Further, longer prompts can damage LLM reasoning and accuracy. Theoretically, the existence of multiple prompts yielding equivalent outputs suggests a high degree of redundancy in the input space, raising fundamental questions about what information is essential to elicit specific model behaviors. We propose three variant frameworks to identify and evaluate minimal prompts and demonstrate that minimal prompts often produce outputs comparable to those of their longer counterparts. These findings suggest new directions for efficient prompt engineering and deepen our understanding of input compression in LLMs.
takeaways: Introduces prompt minimization: reducing prompts to the smallest information-dense form while preserving output fidelity, challenging heuristic prompt design.
Proposes three variant frameworks to identify and evaluate minimal prompts, and reports that minimal prompts often produce outputs comparable to longer prompts.
Implication: shorter prompts can lower inference latency and computational overhead, and may avoid accuracy degradation from overly long contexts.
actionItems: Review the three proposed prompt-minimization frameworks and map how each defines and selects a minimal prompt while preserving output fidelity.
Run a controlled comparison of minimal versus longer prompts on representative tasks, measuring output equivalence, accuracy, and inference latency/computational overhead.
Assess whether prompt minimization is reliable enough for adoption by asking where longer context is still necessary and whether the reported gains hold across different LLMs and tasks.

papers.title: Intent2Tc: Automated Intent-to-Traffic Control Translation with Language Models
papers.authors: Andrea Masini, Sudipta Acharya, Paolo Bellavista, Luca Foschini, Burak Kantarci
papers.abstract: Automated and highly usable Quality-of-Service (QoS) enforcement requires translating high-level service intents into deployable traffic-management policies. Although intent-based networking (IBN) has simplified policy specification, bridging the gap between business-level intents and executable network configurations remains complex, error-prone, and difficult to automate. This paper presents Intent2Tc, a closed-loop language-model-driven framework that translates business-level traffic-shaping intents into declarative sub-intents and subsequently into validated, executable Linux traffic control (tc) configurations. The framework integrates an Active Queue Management (AQM)-based digital twin (DT) semantic model, automated metadata extraction, critique-driven refinement, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)-based knowledge reuse to improve semantic consistency and configuration reliability. We evaluate multiple open-source large language models (LLMs) and small language models (SLMs), together with Claude Sonnet-4.6, on 100 Request for Comments (RFC) 9315-compliant traffic-shaping intents. Across both translation stages, Intent2Tc achieves high semantic fidelity, configuration accuracy, and deployment readiness, with Claude Sonnet-4.6 reaching 0.98 semantic similarity, 1.0 semantic unit coverage, and 0.045 normalized edit distance. Furthermore, RAG reduces token consumption and inference latency while enabling compact models such as Phi-4-mini to approach the performance of substantially larger models. Linux tc serves as the target configuration platform, demonstrating the practical applicability of the proposed framework.
takeaways: Intent2Tc translates business-level traffic-shaping intents into declarative sub-intents and then into executable Linux tc configurations via a closed-loop language-model framework.

The paper evaluates open-source LLMs/SLMs and Claude Sonnet-4.6 on 100 RFC 9315-compliant intents, using an AQM-based digital twin, metadata extraction, critique-driven refinement, and RAG; Claude Sonnet-4.6 reached 0.98 semantic similarity, 1.0 semantic unit coverage, and 0.045 normalized edit distance.

Practically, the approach aims to make QoS enforcement and network policy deployment more automatable, reliable, and usable, while RAG lowers token use and latency and helps compact models approach larger-model performance.
actionItems: Review the closed-loop Intent2Tc pipeline for translating business-level traffic-shaping intents into declarative sub-intents and Linux tc configurations, with attention to the AQM-based digital twin, metadata extraction, critique-driven refinement, and RAG components.

Reproduce the reported evaluation on the 100 RFC 9315-compliant intents by comparing open-source LLMs/SLMs and Claude Sonnet-4.6 on semantic similarity, semantic unit coverage, normalized edit distance, token consumption, and inference latency.

Assess whether the approach is practical for your environment by asking if Linux tc deployment, closed-loop validation, and RAG-based knowledge reuse fit your QoS automation reliability and operational constraints.

papers.title: Improving Visual Sensitivity of LLMs on Multimodal Machine Translation with Metric-based Loss Weighting
papers.authors: Paweł Mąka, Piotr Andruszkiewicz, Yusuf Can Semerci, Jan Scholtes, Gerasimos Spanakis
papers.abstract: Multimodal Machine Translation aims to incorporate additional signal from non-textual modalities to improve translations by resolving ambiguities. While models, through multimodal fusion, are able to accept images related to the source text, they can ignore this information. Therefore, increasing their visual sensitivity remains an active research area. In this work, we introduce a training method, Metric-based Loss Weighting, that improves visual grounding of translations by increasing the loss function for tokens that benefit from the accompanying image. We identify these tokens using the Point-wise Cross-mutual Information (PCXMI) metric, which compares the model's output probabilities with and without visual context. We introduce a Congruency-based PCXMI metric and experimentally show that both metrics working in combination yield the best results. We evaluate our method by fine-tuning three pretrained Multimodal Large Language Models on the task of Image-guided Machine Translation for three language directions. Metric-based Loss Weighting outperforms other tested methods on the CoMMuTE contrastive dataset, improving accuracy by up to more than 7 percentage points compared to standard fine-tuning, while maintaining strong general translation performance.
takeaways: Introduces Metric-based Loss Weighting to improve visual grounding in multimodal machine translation by increasing loss on tokens that benefit from the accompanying image.
Uses Point-wise Cross-mutual Information (PCXMI) and a Congruency-based PCXMI variant to identify image-relevant tokens; the combination gives the best results in experiments.

Fine-tuning three pretrained multimodal LLMs on image-guided machine translation for three language directions improved CoMMuTE accuracy by up to more than 7 points over standard fine-tuning while preserving strong translation performance.
actionItems: Review the Metric-based Loss Weighting and PCXMI-based token selection setup to understand exactly how image-relevant tokens are identified and weighted during multimodal machine translation fine-tuning.
Evaluate the method by reproducing or comparing fine-tuning results on the CoMMuTE contrastive dataset across the three reported language directions and against standard fine-tuning.

Ask whether the extra training complexity and reliance on image-conditioned token scoring is justified for your target multilingual translation pipeline, given the paper’s low applicability and reproducibility signals.

papers.title: Towards Mitigating Fabricated Consensus: The Active Provenance Gate for Multi-Agent Debate Synthesis
papers.abstract: Large language model-based multi-agent debate (MAD) systems are being increasingly used as complex decision pipelines in distributed processes. However, their final synthesis phase still remains inadequately controlled. Even with detailed debate logs, summarizing models are prone to fabricating smoothly written debate consensus that is not grounded in the debate's history. To address this safety gap, this paper presents empirical research and studies if the introduction of active post-debate verification can mitigate the production of such factually unsupported summaries, while still providing valuable information. Furthermore, it is examined whether explicitly signalling divergence is preferable in the absence of a reliable compromise. The Active Provenance Gate (APG) is introduced as a post-debate verification layer that treats the source as a hard constraint, analysing the debate logs, auditing each claim, and applying self-correction. In crisis simulations, the self-healing mechanism more than doubles the average data Provenance Fidelity in difficult condition scenarios, before the strict gate blocks unsupported claims and generates divergence reports. In the human study, a vast majority of the users (over 75%) preferred a report explicitly stating failure in critical scenarios, despite most of them perceiving fabricated consensus from the baseline system as more fluent. Our main contribution is the transition of data origin tracing from passive logging to active conditional blocking before publication.
takeaways: Introduces the Active Provenance Gate (APG), a post-debate verification layer for multi-agent debate synthesis that treats the source as a hard constraint to prevent fabricated consensus.

Uses empirical crisis-simulation tests and a human study: the self-healing mechanism more than doubles average Provenance Fidelity in difficult scenarios, and over 75% of users preferred explicit failure reports in critical cases.

Practical implication: move provenance from passive logging to active conditional blocking before publication, so unsupported claims are filtered and divergence is reported when no reliable compromise exists.
actionItems: Review the APG post-debate verification design and its hard-constraint claim filtering before publication, especially how it audits debate logs and triggers divergence reports.

Evaluate APG in a controlled multi-agent debate benchmark against the baseline using Provenance Fidelity and unsupported-claim blocking rates, including the crisis-simulation and human-preference setup described here.
Assess whether explicit failure/divergence reporting is acceptable for your deployment context when no reliable compromise exists, since the paper reports users preferred it in critical scenarios.
